name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
title: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
answer: Shadow AI in legal teams is the use of generative AI and other machine learning tools by lawyers, paralegals, and support staff without the knowledge or approval of the firm's IT, security, or compliance functions. It typically begins as a productivity shortcut: drafting emails, summarizing depositions, or researching case law through a consumer chat interface. Because these tools sit outside the firm's sanctioned software inventory, they bypass procurement review, data loss prevention, and conflict checking. The scope includes both individual use and team-level informal adoption, and it cuts across practice areas from litigation to transactional work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Shadow AI usually runs on personal devices, personal accounts, and public cloud services rather than the firm's managed infrastructure. Common entry points are browser based chat assistants, mobile apps, and browser extensions installed without administrator rights. Data entered into these tools may be processed on servers outside the firm's jurisdiction or retained for model training under terms the firm never reviewed. There is often no single sign-on, no e-discovery hold, and no logging that the firm's security team can access.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by pasting client documents, emails, or case notes into an unapproved tool and asking it to summarize, draft, or analyze. Lawyers may also use shadow AI for document review, contract clause extraction, or deposition preparation without telling the partner or client. Because the tool is not connected to the firm's document management system, the output is copied back manually, and the prompt history lives only in the user's personal account. This creates a gap between the official matter file and the actual work product.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are loss of attorney-client privilege, breach of confidentiality, and violation of data protection or bar rules. If client data is submitted to a third party without client consent or a proper vendor agreement, privilege may be waived or the firm may face regulatory exposure. Provenance is weak because there is no audit trail linking the AI output to the source documents or the model version. Firms need clear policies, training, and technical controls that detect and block unsanctioned AI use while offering approved alternatives.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Legal teams are moving from outright prohibition to managed enablement, where the firm provides a sanctioned AI workspace with approved models, logging, and data residency controls. Security audits are beginning to include shadow AI discovery as a standard control, using browser telemetry, network logs, and data loss prevention alerts. Over time, the distinction between shadow AI and approved AI will blur as firms integrate AI into document management and practice management systems. The goal is to capture the productivity benefit without losing the evidentiary and ethical safeguards that legal work requires.
